He may be a hypocrite, but that doesn't invalidate his original point. Clarity of speech is important, but so is a willingness to listen attentively.

I for one think that expressing complex points of view is a lot harder than what people make it out to be, especially on day-to-day discussion. People need to cut a lot of slack about clarity of speech - yes, it is very important but also hard as fuck so people should be largely patient as their discussion partners try to elaborate their points.

In scenarios where people are gathering to discuss specific ideas this seems less important because often the prerequisites and concepts have already been laid out beforehand - for example, when a philosopher goes to make a lecture in a university hall or a worker's advocate goes to make a speech before an union. Everyone there is supposed to know the basics or at the very least should be ready to be open-minded and assume ignorance instead of immediately assuming the speaker is spitting non-sense or false pretenses. Similarly, in books (or Internet comments) the writer can carefully expose concepts and choose the structure and flow of text without interruption.

I think this is a very big problem because the common folk is likely to never once in their life have tried to communicate a truly complex concept, so they jump at every opportunity to make the scholar invalidated based not on the quality of his ideas but on the possible slipping of his rhetoric. We see this go wild on political debates (among politicians and common folk alike): as soon as someone makes a semantic error, the simple-minded is fast to "prove" his entire discourse wrong based on the smallest slip of the tongue and likely hold on to that for years to come as "proof" that the other side is completely moronic and unfounded. It's really counter-productive.

If you think in complex terms expressing yourself is one of the hardest things in life, as is communicating meaningful ideas - even more so when the listener isn't on par intellectually.
